claims.text: Local compositional disorder in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles induces surface atomic strain.
Disorder-induced surface strain lowers the effective cohesive energy.
The reduction in effective cohesive energy governs premelting and overall melting behavior.
Local compositional variations and chemical heterogeneity generate surface atomic strain.
Enhanced surface strain caused by compositional disorder reduces effective bond strength.
Reduced effective bond strength promotes early surface disorder or premelting.
Early surface disorder leads to a lower complete melting temperature than in more homogeneously mixed nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater local compositional disorder will have greater surface strain.
Nanoparticles with greater local compositional disorder will exhibit an earlier onset of premelting than homogeneous controls.
Nanoparticles with greater local compositional disorder will have a lower complete melting temperature than homogeneous controls.
Uniform, randomly mixed nanoparticles should premelt at temperatures consistent with conventional melting models.
The baseline melting behavior reflects the nanoparticles' average cohesive-energy distribution.
The proposed relationship should hold for nanoparticles containing four to six principal elements and measuring 5–50 nm.
Oxidation or other additional phenomena may cause deviations from the proposed relationship.
Theory supports a qualitative connection among compositional disorder, surface strain, and melting behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis ambiguously equates compositional disorder with spatial chemical heterogeneity or partial segregation while also describing a uniform random alloy as the low-disorder baseline. Atomic-scale random mixing is itself compositional disorder, whereas partial segregation can reduce randomness while increasing mesoscale heterogeneity. The proposed comparison therefore does not consistently define or order the independent variable.
